steps.line: Tomorrow you speak in court, five charges to answer in order. Keep them here, not on a scroll.
Walk the colonnade from the door. At each place, set one strange picture of one charge.

steps.text: Go to the first empty place

steps.act: Set the first image: a man on fire (the arson)
Set the second: a goat in a toga (the forged will)
Set the third: a huge ear (the witness who overheard)
Set the fourth: a bloody knife (the assault)

steps.text: The next place, by the golden hand

steps.act: Set the fifth: a donkey in a crown (the bribe)

steps.line: Five places, five pictures. The stranger they are, the longer they stay.

steps.text: Go to the court in the Forum, and stand where the advocate stands

steps.line: The praetor nods. Speak. Walk your house again, from the door, and read your pictures in order.

steps.text: Walk your places again, in order

steps.act: Speak the fifth charge, and close

steps.line: Every charge answered, in order, without a scroll. Do it again tomorrow, and the next day.
The vultures have given you the hill. Yoke the white ox and the white cow, and mark the line of the wall.

steps.act: Drive the furrow round the hill

steps.line: “Remus, in derision of his brother, leaped over the new walls.”
Your brother stands inside your line, laughing.
“So perish every one that shall hereafter leap over my wall.” Romulus held the city alone.
Your father's army and your husband's stand face to face in the valley. You were taken from the one and married to the other.
“The Sabine women, from the outrage on whom the war originated, with hair dishevelled and garments rent...”
“Turn your anger on us. We are the cause of the war: better that we perish than live widowed or orphaned.”
Both armies lower their spears. The kings make peace and one city of two peoples. Rome has learned its way of growing.
Lucretia has told them what Sextus Tarquin did, made them swear vengeance, and said: “no unchaste woman shall live by my example.”
“She plunged a knife, which she kept concealed beneath her garment, into her heart.”
Her father and her husband are overwhelmed with grief. You have played the fool all your life so that the king would not fear you.

steps.act: Draw the knife from the wound

steps.line: “By this blood, most pure before the outrage of a prince, I swear that I will pursue Lucius Tarquinius Superbus and all his race...”
“...nor will I suffer them or any other to be king in Rome.” You hand them the knife; they swear it too.
They carry her body to the forum of Collatia. The kings have reigned two hundred and forty-four years; the Republic begins tonight.
This small river is the border of your province. Cross it with your army, and you are at war with Rome.
“Computing how many calamities his passing that river would bring upon mankind, and what a relation of it would be transmitted...”

steps.act: Stand on the bank, and weigh it

steps.line: “At last, in a sort of passion, casting aside calculation, and abandoning himself to what might come...”

steps.act: Say it: the die is cast

steps.line: “He took the river.” Whatever follows, you cannot now go back.
The feast of the Lupercalia. You sit on the Rostra in a golden chair, in triumphal robes, and Antony runs up from the race.
“Antony... brought him a diadem wreathed with laurel.” A few clap, as arranged. The crowd is silent.
Everyone cheers. Antony offers it again. A few clap; the rest are silent.
“The people followed his refusal with great shouts.” You send the diadem to the Capitol, to Jupiter, the only king in Rome.
You have refused the name. You keep the thing. Rome has seen the difference, and some of them are counting the days.
The Ides of March. A soothsayer said beware this day; Calpurnia dreamed; you came anyway. The Senate sits in Pompey's hall.
“The senators who were not in the plot were astonished and dared neither fly nor assist Caesar, nor so much as speak a word.”
Tillius Cimber comes with a petition for his brother. The others press round, as if to join him. He pulls your toga from your neck.
“Casca gave him the first cut, in the neck, which was not mortal nor dangerous.” You seize his hand: Casca, what are you doing?

steps.act: Look at them, one by one

steps.line: Daggers on every side. “When he saw Brutus's sword drawn, he covered his face with his robe and submitted.”

steps.act: Pull your toga over your face

steps.line: You fall at the foot of Pompey's statue, with twenty-three wounds. The pedestal runs with blood: Pompey presides over the vengeance.
Troy is burning. Hector's ghost told you to take the gods of the city and go. Your father will not leave his house.
“And die with me? Must I? He said no more. An omen on the boy's head changed his mind.” Now he will come, if you carry him.
“Haste, my dear father, 'tis no time to wait, and load my shoulders with a willing freight.” He carries the household gods.
“My hand shall lead our little son; and you, my faithful consort, shall our steps pursue.” Creusa follows behind.

steps.text: Make for the gate, through the fire

steps.line: “Alas! I lost Creusa.” You went back into the burning city and found only her shade, who told you to go on. You went on.
The Sibyl: “the gates of hell are open night and day; smooth the descent, and easy is the way: but to return... there the labour lies.”
“In the neighb'ring grove there stands a tree; the queen of Stygian realms has claimed it for her own. A golden bough...”
“If fate has chosen you, it comes away in your hand; if not, no force can tear it.” Two doves of your mother show you the tree.

steps.text: Follow the doves to the tree

steps.line: It comes away. “He seized the shining bough with greedy hand and bore it to the Sibyl's cave.”

steps.text: Go down to the cave's mouth

steps.line: Below are the Styx, the unburied dead, Dido who will not speak to you, and your father among the souls to come. You have your way back.
Turnus is down, your spear through his thigh. The Rutulians groan. He raises his hand to you.
“I ask not life... but if you can be moved by a father's grief, pity old Daunus, and send me, or my body, back to my own.”
“In deep suspense the Trojan seem'd to stand, and, just prepar'd to strike, repress'd his hand.”
On his shoulder, the belt of Pallas, the boy Evander gave into your care, whom Turnus killed and stripped. The studs shine in the sun.
“Then, rous'd anew to wrath, he loudly cries... Pallas, with this sword, Pallas takes vengeance, and from your blood exacts his due.”
“The streaming blood distain'd his arms around, and the disdainful soul came rushing thro' the wound.” The poem ends here.

the_sunbeam.title: The sunbeam, On the Nature of Things I

steps.line: Lucretius says there are bodies too small to see, and a void for them to move in. Go and look, in a dark room.

steps.act: Watch the motes in the beam

steps.line: “The winds beat upon the sea and overwhelm huge ships, and yet are unseen bodies.”
“A ring on the finger is thinned by wearing, the dripping water hollows the stone, the ploughshare wastes away in the fields.”
“Nature works by unseen bodies.” And the dark round the beam is the void: where there is no room, nothing could move at all.

nothing_to_us.title: Death is nothing to us, On the Nature of Things III

steps.line: The road out of the gate is lined with tombs. Read one: I was not, I was, I am not, I care not.
“Death therefore is nothing to us, concerns us not a jot, since the nature of the mind is proved to be mortal.”
“When we shall be no more, when there shall have been a separation of body and soul, nothing can happen to us who shall then be no more.”
The man who fears being a corpse has left a bit of himself standing by to weep. There will be no one there.
“Nor by prolonging life do we take one tittle from the time past in death.” Go back into the garden. The sun is still out.
You are Regulus, consul, captured by Carthage. They sent you to Rome to ask for an exchange of prisoners, on your oath to return.
“He gave it as his opinion that the prisoners should not be returned: they were young men and good warriors, while he was bowed with age.”
His family and friends begged him to stay. He had sworn. Cicero: he preferred to return to torture rather than break his word.
The Carthaginians are waiting. Beyond the gate are the eyelids cut off, the sleepless days, the death. You know it.
“He did not hesitate to go back, well knowing what he was going to.” Nothing is expedient that is not honourable; that was the proof.
You talked of Africanus with the old king until late. Now, in sleep, he comes to you, in the form you know from his bust.
“Be firm, Scipio, and do not be afraid.” He shows you Carthage, which you will destroy, and tells you your years.
He takes you up. “A high place, full of stars, shining and splendid.” The whole of things lies below you.
“The earth itself appeared to me so small, that it grieved me to think of our empire, with which we cover but a point of it.”
A sound, loud and sweet: nine spheres turning, each with its note. “The ears of men are deaf to it, as those by the Nile's cataracts.”
“How long will your mind be fixed on the ground? Do you not see what regions you have come into?”
“For all who have preserved, aided or enlarged their country there is a sure and fixed place in heaven.” Exercise your soul in that.
He is gone, and the sleep with him. You lie on Masinissa's couch in the dark, with the stars where they were.
Cupid shot you with the gold arrow and her with the lead. You have chased her down the valley; she is at her father's river.
“Her strength being spent, she grows pale, and overcome with the fatigue of so swift a flight, looks upon the waters of Peneus...”
“Destroy, by changing it, this shape of mine, by which I have pleased too much.”
“A heavy torpor seizes her limbs; her soft breasts are covered with a thin bark; her hair grows into leaves, her arms into branches...”

steps.act: Lay your hand on the bark

steps.line: “He feels her heart still throb beneath the new bark.” You take the laurel for your tree. She bends her top, as if nodding.
You sang before the king and queen of the dead, and the shades wept. They gave her back on one condition.
“He may not turn back his eyes until he has passed the Avernian valleys, or the gift will be void.”
She walks behind you, slowed by her wound. You must not look. The way up is steep, dark and silent.

steps.text: Lead her up, without looking back

steps.line: The light is close. “Fearing that she might fail him, and eager to see her, he turned his eyes.”
“Immediately she sank back; stretching out her arms, she caught nothing but the yielding air.”
“Dying a second time, she made no complaint of her husband; for what could she complain of, except that she was loved?”

steps.text: Go out into the light, alone

steps.line: You have seen the women of Cyprus and wanted none of them. You carved one in snow-white ivory, and she is better than any of them.
“He gives it kisses, and thinks they are returned; he speaks to it, he embraces it, he brings it presents: shells, pebbles, little birds.”
At the feast of Venus you prayed, not daring to say the statue, for a wife like my ivory girl. The altar's flame leapt three times.
“She seemed to be warm.”

steps.act: Press your hand to her breast

steps.line: “The ivory grows soft, and losing its hardness, yields to the fingers, as the wax of Hymettus grows soft in the sun.”
“She felt the kisses, and blushed, and raising her timid eyes to the light, saw at once her lover and the sky.”
The last of the free peoples of Britain stand on this hill. Below, the Romans have drawn up. You are Calgacus; they ask you to speak.
“There is no people beyond us, nothing but waves and rocks, and the Romans, more deadly still, whose arrogance no submission escapes.”
“Robbers of the world: if the enemy is rich, they are greedy; if poor, they are ambitious; neither East nor West has satisfied them.”
“To plunder, to slaughter, to steal, these things they call empire; and where they make a desert, they call it peace.”
The host answered with a shout. Then the battle, and the rout; and the next day a great silence, the hills empty, the houses smoking.
Tacitus put these words in your mouth. He was a Roman senator, and the son-in-law of the man who won the day. He knew they were true.

ours_and_not_ours.title: Ours and not ours, Encheiridion I

steps.line: Two baskets on the table. The left for what is not in our power, the right for what is. Epictetus hands you the first thing: your body.

steps.text: Put it in the left basket

steps.line: “Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices, and in a word, whatever are not our own acts.” Now: your opinion of it.
“In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, and in a word, whatever are our acts.” Now: your reputation.
And last: what you will do about all this.
“If you think that only which is your own to be your own, no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you; you will have no enemy.”

steps.text: Lie down on the camp bed

steps.line: It is not yet light. Your body does not want to get up. You are the emperor; the letters are already waiting, and the Danube.
“Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.”
“All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.”
“I can neither be injured by any of them... nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for co-operation.”
“Like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.” The secretary is there with the letters. Begin.
“Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things.”

steps.text: Go to the bench by the fountain

steps.line: “But this is a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.”
“For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul.”
“Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental.”
The letters are still waiting. You go back to them a little quieter. That is all the retreat there is, and it is enough.

the_ledger_of_years.title: The ledger of years, On the Shortness of Life III

steps.line: Paulinus measures the city's grain on this floor, sack by sack. Seneca asks you to measure something else: your years.

steps.act: Count the years a creditor took
Count the years a patron took, and the years you waited at his door
Count the years a quarrel took, and a mistress, and wandering about the city

steps.line: “Call to mind how often you have been sure of your plans; how few days have passed as you intended; when you were at your own disposal.”
“You will find that you are dying before your time.”
“No one will bring back your years; no one will restore you to yourself. Life will go on as it began, and will not turn back.”
“We do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them.”
Seneca to Paulinus: leave the corn to others, and withdraw to the quiet now, while there is time. He wrote it; he did not do it.
